unit.title: Support, resistance and chart patterns
unit.description: Price zones, trendlines, chart patterns and false breakouts

texts: The floor that became a ceiling
Laura
A support at €30 held for a year. One day, the price closes at €27 on heavy volume.
Now it’s bouncing back to €30. It’s bound to go up again like before!
What’s most likely at €30?
It goes straight through
Now there are sellers at €30: the people who bought at support want out.
It runs into selling: the old support can act as resistance
Exactly! It’s **role reversal**. It’s not guaranteed, but it’s worth watching.
The level no longer matters
Quite the opposite: broken levels matter even more. Lots of people remember them.
So what used to be a floor can now be a ceiling…
And the other way round: broken resistance often turns into **support**.
Floor or ceiling, after the break?
A broken level doesn’t disappear: it **switches roles**. Place each case.
New support
New resistance
Resistance broken upwards on volume
What used to stop the rises now tends to stop the falls.
Support lost on heavy volume
Whoever bought there will want to get out «without a loss» if the price comes back: selling shows up.
The year’s high, cleared on volume
Whoever sold at that ceiling will want to buy back if the price returns.
A multi-month low, lost on volume
The old floor tends to cap the bounces.
€50 ceiling broken; weeks later, the price comes back to €50
It’s the return to the level: if it holds as a floor, the breakout gains credibility.
€30 floor broken; the price bounces back to €30
It’s Laura’s case: the old floor acts as a ceiling.
Place all six cases.
Broken support often becomes **resistance**, and broken resistance becomes **support**. Yesterday’s ceiling can be the new floor.
Hint: think about who wants to get out «without a loss» at that level.
Nice! Notice which way each level broke.
Place each case: floor or ceiling?

steps.title: The return to the level
steps.body:
After a breakout, the price often comes back to **test** the level before moving on. Bulkowski calls it a *throwback* if the breakout was upwards and a *pullback* if it was downwards. In the head and shoulders, for example, the price returns to the neckline **68 %** of the time.

If the broken level holds on the return, the breakout gains credibility. If the price clearly moves back inside, the breakout was false and the idea has failed.
steps.key: Broken support often becomes resistance, and broken resistance becomes support.
steps.tip: Try it: in Market, set a price alert at an old ceiling that has already broken.

texts: Does the trend hold?
Four real trends, with no name or date. Imagine a line through the lows or the highs. Does it go up or down in the next 10 sessions?
Play all four rounds.
Here, two trends continued and two broke. A **trendline** doesn't predict the future: it marks **where the idea stops being valid**.
Two continued and two turned. The line warns you of the change.
Follow the direction by eye and decide
A good line or a forced one?
A **trendline** connects the price’s turning points. Sort them.
Valid uptrend line
Valid downtrend line
Forced or fragile
Connects two higher lows and a third one touches it
Two higher lows draw it; the third touch confirms it.
Connects three successively lower highs
A downtrend line connects lower highs above the price.
It cuts through several candles to fit
If you have to force it, the line is in your head, not on the chart.
Almost vertical after a 40 % rise in three weeks
Very steep lines break quickly; those at around 30–45 degrees last longer.
Connects two lower highs
Two lower highs are already enough to draw it.
Rises at a moderate slope with three touches
A moderate slope with several touches is the most sustainable.
Sort all six lines.
An **uptrend** line connects higher lows; a **downtrend** line, lower highs. Two points draw it, the third confirms it, and you **never force it**.
Hint: uptrend lines run below the price, along the lows.
You’re doing well. Watch out for the ones that look too perfect.
Sort each line
The line broke
Leo
The share has broken its uptrend line. It’s over, I’m selling everything!
The price is still above its last relevant low.
What do you tell Leo?
He’s right: a downtrend is starting
Not always: breaking the line may only lead to a **sideways** phase.
He should check the structure of highs and lows too
That’s it! A line break is read together with the highs and lows.
He should redraw the line until it fits again
Forcing the line is fooling yourself. Better to look at the highs and lows.
OK, I won’t sell over a line. I’ll watch whether it loses the last low.
Breaking the line is a warning, not a verdict.

steps.title: Channels and slope
steps.body:
A parallel line through the highs of an uptrend forms a **channel**: the lower edge acts as support and the upper edge as resistance.

Very steep lines break quickly; those at around **30–45 degrees** tend to hold longer. On charts covering several years, use a **logarithmic scale**.
steps.key: An uptrend line connects higher lows; as long as it holds, the trend continues.
steps.tip: Try it: in Market, draw a «Trend line» through two rising lows on Apple.

texts: Sell before the break?
Pablo
Look: after a big rise, two shoulders and a head. A textbook head and shoulders!
It hasn’t broken the neckline yet, but I’m selling now to get ahead.
What do you tell him?
Good: getting ahead always pays
No break, no pattern: many end up making new highs.
The pattern doesn’t exist until it closes below the neckline
That’s it! And even once confirmed, it fails **19 %** of the time.
He should buy more: the pattern is bullish
The normal H&S is bearish. The **inverse** one, after a fall, is the bullish one.
The **neckline** connects the lows between the peaks. Breaking it confirms the pattern.
Is there a pattern yet?
Three peaks aren’t enough. Decide what each case is.
H&S (bearish)
Inverse H&S (bullish)
Not a pattern yet
After a rise: three peaks, the middle one highest, and a close below the neckline
All in order: a prior rise, a higher head and a break with a close.
After a fall: three lows, the middle one lowest, and a close above the neckline
It’s the bullish version: it appears after a fall and breaks upwards.
Two shoulders and a head, with the price still above the neckline
Without a break, it’s only a possibility.
Three peaks after a rise and just a wick below the neckline
A wick confirms nothing: you need a close.
Three lows after a fall, with the price still below the neckline
The inverse one also needs to break its neckline, upwards.
Sort all five cases.
Without a **close on the other side of the neckline**, there’s no pattern. An H&S without a break is just a nicely shaped mountain.
Always look for the same thing: is there a close on the other side of the neckline?
Very good. Look at what came before, too: a rise or a fall?
Read each case and decide

steps.title: The target and the data
steps.body:
Classic target: the distance from the head to the neckline, projected from the break. Head at €120, neckline at €100: height €20 → target **€80**. Bulkowski suggests a more cautious one, using half the height → **€90**.

His data: average fall after the break, **16 %**; fails (doesn’t even fall 5 %), **19 %**; returns to the neckline, **68 %**; reaches the classic target, only **51 %**.
steps.tip: Try it: in Market, look for three peaks on a weekly chart and mark their neckline.

texts: Two peaks
Ana
Two almost identical highs: a double top! I’m selling before it drops.
The price is still above the low of the trough between the two peaks.
What mistake is Ana making?
None: she’s ahead of everyone
She’s jumping ahead of a pattern that doesn’t exist yet. Many are just pauses.
She’s anticipating an unconfirmed pattern
That’s it! A double top is confirmed when the price **breaks the trough**. Before that, it’s just two peaks.
She’s selling too late
The opposite: she’s selling before she has confirmation.
Many «double tops in the making» turn out to be pauses before new highs.
Confirmed or just possible?
A double top is shaped like an **M**, a double bottom like a **W**. Which ones are confirmed?
Confirmed
Just possible
Two similar highs and a close below the trough
A double top is confirmed when a close breaks the low of the trough.
Two similar highs and the price still above the trough
Without a break of the trough, all you have is two peaks.
Two similar lows and a close above the high in between
A double bottom is confirmed when the price clears the high in between.
Two similar lows and a wick that touches the high in between
A wick isn’t enough: you need a close on the other side.
A W shape, with the price halfway to the high in between
It looks like a double bottom, but it hasn’t cleared its key line yet.
Sort all five cases.
Double top (**M**): confirmed when the price **breaks the trough**; double bottom (**W**): when it **clears the high in between**. Always with a close, not a wick.
Always ask yourself: has it closed on the other side of the key line?
Nice! The shape isn’t enough: the break is what counts.
Read each case: confirmed or just possible?

steps.title: The target
steps.body:
Classic target: the height of the pattern, projected from the breakout.

Double bottom with lows at €40 and a high in between at €50. Height: €10. On a close above €50, the classic target is **€60**. If it then closes clearly below €50 again, the breakout has failed.
steps.tip: Try it: if you spot an M in Market, set a price alert at its trough.

texts: Pauses on real candles
Four real charts: can you spot a pause after a strong move? Decide whether it goes up or down over the next 10 sessions.
Answer all four rounds.
After a strong move, the price often **catches its breath** for a few days. These pauses have names (triangles, flags, rectangles), but **they don't tell you how they end**.
Done. Getting four rounds right or wrong says very little.
You’re doing well… but the pause doesn’t tell you how it ends.
Look at the candles and choose: up or down?
Which way does it usually break?
These pauses are **continuation patterns**. Their shape tells you who’s pushing.
Usually breaks upwards
Usually breaks downwards
Either way
Ascending triangle: flat ceiling and higher lows
Buyers push up from below against a fixed ceiling.
Descending triangle: flat floor and lower highs
Sellers push down from above against a fixed floor.
Symmetrical triangle: lower highs and higher lows
Nobody’s in control: the breakout decides.
Rectangle: flat ceiling and flat floor
It’s a sideways range: a breakout on volume sets the direction.
Flag after a bullish flagpole, in a bull market
According to Bulkowski, it breaks upwards 60 % of the time.
Sort all five patterns.
The **ascending** and **descending** triangles have a bias; the symmetrical triangle and the rectangle depend on the breakout. **Volume** tends to fall while they form and rise when they break.
Hint: the flat line is the one someone is defending. Who’s pushing against it?
Well spotted. The shape gives clues, not certainties.
Sort each pattern

steps.title: Flags and rectangles
steps.body:
• **Flag:** after a strong, fast move (the **flagpole**), a few days in a small rectangle tilted against the trend. It lasts **less than 3 weeks**. If it’s a small triangle, it’s a **pennant**.
• **Rectangle:** a sideways range between clear support and resistance.

Bulkowski: in a bull market, flags break upwards **60 %** of the time, the average move after the breakout is around **9 %** and they **fail** (don’t even advance 5 %) in roughly **44–45 %** of cases.
steps.key: Continuation patterns are the market catching its breath, although sometimes it turns.
steps.tip: Try it: in Market, mark Bitcoin's latest pause with «Rectangle».

texts: Marta’s breakout
Marta
Resistance at €100. Today the price reaches €101.50 during the session.
It’s broken out! I’m buying at €101 before it gets away.
At the close: €99.20, on low volume.
What happened?
She bought a confirmed breakout
No: it closed below the level with no volume. It was a wick.
She bought an excursion that wasn’t confirmed
That’s it! No close above and no volume means no breakout: it’s a **false breakout**.
The right move: you have to get in before anyone else
Getting in before confirmation is the classic way to fall for a false breakout.
So what do I do now?
If she has a stop, the mistake costs her little. Without one, she can end up trapped.
Filters against false breakouts
If you buy the breakout and the price falls back inside, you’re **trapped**. What protects you and what walks you into the trap?
Filters out false breakouts
Walks you into the trap
Waiting for a close on the other side of the level
A close says far more than a wick that lasts a few hours.
Asking for above-average volume
With volume, lots of people are behind the move.
Requiring the close to clear the level by 1–3 %
An extra margin filters out lots of excursions.
Jumping in on the first wick that pokes through
That’s exactly what traps most people in false breakouts.
Checking whether the broken level holds on the return
If the old ceiling holds as a floor, the breakout gains credibility.
Buying because a forum is shouting «it’s broken out!»
Other people’s euphoria confirms nothing.
Sort all six ideas.
A breakout is confirmed by the **close** and the **volume**, not by the wick. And no filter gets rid of them all: according to Bulkowski, the H&S fails 19 % of the time and flags around 44 %.
Hint: what takes patience usually filters; what rushes you, traps you.
Nice! You’ve already got half your list of filters.
Sort each idea

steps.title: And if it fails, the stop
steps.body: No filter gets rid of them all. That’s why the stop goes where the breakout stops making sense: back inside the zone, below the last relevant low. And the position size is set so that this failure costs little.
steps.key: A breakout without a close or volume is just an excursion.
steps.tip: Try it: after your next purchase, set a price alert where the idea fails.

u21l2-3.prompt: Bruno bought after resistance at €100 was broken. The price rises to €106 and falls back to €101. What’s the sensible thing to do?
options: Buy three times as much to average down
Sell in a panic: it’s all over
Watch whether €100 holds as support; his stop was already below that zone
u21l2-3.explanation: Returning to the broken level is normal; what matters is whether it holds.
feedback: Adding more without a plan in the middle of the uncertainty multiplies the risk.
Retesting the broken level is very common. If it holds above €100, the breakout is still alive.
Good: if the old ceiling holds as a floor, the idea is still valid; if it closes clearly back inside, the breakout was false.

u21l2-4.prompt: You’ve bought at the last price. Place the stop where the idea stops being valid: below the last relevant low.
u21l2-4.explanation: Below the recent low, the structure that justified buying breaks down.

u21l2-5.prompt: Place the target at the previous high, where selling appeared before.
u21l2-5.explanation: The previous high is resistance: it’s reasonable to expect selling there and take profits.

u21l2-6.prompt: No name, no date. Up or down over the next 10 sessions?
u21l2-6.explanation: A level switching roles is common, not guaranteed. That’s why every idea comes with a stop on the other side of the level.

u21l2-7.prompt: Another real chart. Up or down over the next 10 sessions?
u21l2-7.explanation: Levels help you decide where to get in and where to get out if you’re wrong; they don’t predict the outcome.

u21l2-10.prompt: When the price breaks out upwards and then returns to the broken level, Bulkowski calls it a ____.
u21l2-10.explanation: After a downside breakout, the return is called a pullback.

u21l3-2.prompt: Look at the lows: what trend do they show? (Apple · closes every 3 sessions · July–September 2025)
u21l3-2.explanation: Each low is above the previous one: you could draw an uptrend line underneath.

u21l3-3.prompt: Now look at the highs: what trend do they show? (Nike · closes every 3 sessions · August–October 2026)
u21l3-3.explanation: The highs keep getting lower: a downtrend line would connect them from above.

u21l3-4.prompt: To draw the downtrend line you need the starting point: tap the highest close (ASML · closes every 3 sessions · February–April 2025)
u21l3-4.explanation: It’s the first close: from there, each high was lower. The downtrend line would connect that peak with the following highs.

u21l3-5.prompt: In this rise, tap the lowest close: the start of the uptrend line (ASML · closes every 3 sessions · May–July 2026)
u21l3-5.explanation: From that low, each dip stopped higher: it’s the line’s first anchor point.

u21l3-7.prompt: Which scale is best for drawing trendlines over several years?
u21l3-7.explanation: On a linear scale, an exponential trend seems to break its line when it doesn’t.

u21l3-8.prompt: If you draw a parallel line through the highs of an uptrend, you get a ____.
u21l3-8.explanation: Inside the channel, the lower edge acts as support and the upper edge as resistance.

u21l3-11.prompt: You buy within an uptrend. Place the stop below the last relevant low, the one holding up your line.
u21l3-11.explanation: If the price loses the last low, the line and the structure of rising lows break at the same time: the idea no longer holds. Right above it, any normal dip would take you out.

u21l3-12.prompt: An uptrend line has three touches. The price drops to touch it a fourth time and Marta wants to buy without a stop «because it always bounces». What do you tell her?
options: That she can buy, but with the stop below the line and the last low
To redraw the line lower so she can relax
That she's right: three touches are a guarantee
u21l3-12.explanation: A trendline tells you where the idea stops being valid. That's why the stop goes on the other side: if it breaks, you get out losing little.
feedback: That's it: if the line breaks and loses the low, she gets out with a small loss.
Moving the line to make it fit is fooling yourself: the line is on the chart, not in her wishes.
Three touches make the line more relevant, not unbreakable. Lines get broken all the time.

u21l4-1.prompt: Put the formation of a head and shoulders in order.
options: Right shoulder, lower than the head
u21l4-1.explanation: The pattern only exists once the last step arrives: the neckline break.

u21l4-6.prompt: Before looking for shoulders, find the summit: tap the highest close in this stretch (Airbus · closes every 3 sessions · July–August 2025)
u21l4-6.explanation: In an H&S, the head would be that peak. But to call it a pattern you’d need two lower shoulders and, above all, a neckline break.

u21l4-8.prompt: Nasdaq 100, March 2000, after years of strong gains. What do you think happened next?
u21l4-8.explanation: Reversal patterns are confirmed when their key line breaks, and you only see that afterwards. At the top, nobody has that confirmation yet.

u21l4-11.prompt: You own shares in a company. After a big rise it forms a head and shoulders and today closes below the neckline on high volume. What do you do?
options: Nothing: patterns fail, so I ignore them
I buy more: it's cheaper now
I review my plan: sell part or protect my gains, because the pattern has been confirmed
u21l4-11.explanation: A confirmed pattern isn't a certainty, but it changes the plan: according to Bulkowski, the average fall after the breakout is 16 %.
feedback: They fail 19 % of the time, not almost always: a confirmed pattern is a serious warning.
Buying more just as a bearish pattern is confirmed means going against the signal.
That's it: the breakout confirms the pattern. It's not certain to fall, but you now have a reason to act according to plan.

u21l4-12.prompt: Confirmed head and shoulders, with the head at €120 and the neckline at €100. Ana is waiting for it to fall to the classic target of €80 to buy back in. What do you tell her?
options: That only half reach €80: a prudent target would be €90
That the pattern gives no clue about how far it falls
That it'll surely reach €80: it's the pattern's target
u21l4-12.explanation: Pattern targets are references, not promises. With half the height, the target is more realistic.
feedback: That's it: Bulkowski suggests half the height, €90, because the full target is only reached 51 % of the time.
It does give a reference: the height projected from the breakout. But it's a reference, not a promise.
According to Bulkowski, only 51 % reach the classic target.

u21l4-13.prompt: What do you reply to Lumi?
options: It's an inverse H&S: bullish, and it's confirmed when it closes above its neckline
Yes: all head and shoulders patterns are bearish
It's bullish: I'll buy now, before the breakout
u21l4-13.explanation: The normal H&S comes after a rise and is bearish; the inverse one comes after a fall and is bullish. Both are confirmed when they break their neckline.
feedback: That's it: after a fall, the inverse version points upwards. And without a breakout, it isn't a pattern yet.
This one is upside down and comes after a fall: it's the inverse one, which is bullish.
Right direction, but without a close above the neckline the pattern doesn't exist.
lines: After months of falling I see three lows, with the middle one lowest.
It's a head and shoulders: bearish, right?

u21l5-7.prompt: Tap the lowest close in this stretch: in a double bottom, it would be one of the two lows (Siemens · closes every 3 sessions · February–April 2026)
u21l5-7.explanation: Buyers showed up there and the price bounced. To call it a double bottom you’d need a second similar low and a break above the high in between.

u21l5-8.prompt: Look at the latest highs and lows. Up or down over the next 10 sessions?
u21l5-8.explanation: A half-formed pattern is only a hypothesis. Until it breaks its key line, it could go either way.

u21l5-9.prompt: Another real chart, no name. Up or down over the next 10 sessions?
u21l5-9.explanation: Looking for Ms and Ws on every chart is tempting; the eye finds shapes everywhere. That’s why a breakout is required.

u21l5-11.prompt: Double bottom with lows at €40 and an intermediate high at €50. The price closes at €51 and Bruno buys. Days later it closes at €47. What has happened?
options: The breakout has failed: it has closed clearly below €50 again
u21l5-11.explanation: A confirmed pattern can still fail. If the price closes clearly back on the other side of the key line, the breakout was false.
feedback: Buying more into an idea that has failed usually makes the loss bigger.
The target only counts if the breakout holds, and it has closed clearly below €50 again.
That's it: if it goes back inside the pattern with a clear close, the idea no longer holds. Time to get out as planned.

u21l5-12.prompt: Same double bottom: lows at €40, intermediate high at €50 and a close at €51. Where does Bruno's stop make most sense?
options: A little below €50, where the breakout would fail
No need: the pattern is confirmed
u21l5-12.explanation: The stop goes where the idea stops being valid. In a breakout, that means back inside the pattern.
feedback: That's it: if it closes clearly below €50 again, the idea has failed and he gets out losing little.
It makes sense, but it's very far away: he risks much more per share for the same idea.
Confirmed doesn't mean certain. Without a stop, a failure can cost a lot.

u21l5-13.prompt: Now with real candles: you've bought at the last price. Place the stop below the last relevant low, as under the bottoms of a W.
u21l5-13.explanation: Below the recent low, the structure that justified the purchase breaks. A little margin stops a mere wick from taking you out.

u21l6-1.prompt: Match each pattern with its shape.
u21l6-1.explanation: The shape tells you who’s pushing: in the ascending one, the buyers; in the descending one, the sellers.

u21l6-2.prompt: Match each part with its definition.
u21l6-2.explanation: Flagpole, pause and breakout: that’s the story of a continuation pattern.
right: Small rectangle tilted against the trend
Exit from the pattern, ideally on volume

u21l6-4.prompt: A rectangle is a sideways range. What trend does this stretch have? (Nike · closes every 3 sessions · April–May 2024)
u21l6-4.explanation: The price swings between a ceiling and a floor and ends up almost where it started: that’s what a rectangle looks like.

u21l6-5.prompt: According to Bulkowski, what percentage of flags fail (don’t even advance 5 %) in bull markets?
u21l6-5.explanation: They’re short-range patterns: almost half don’t even reach 5 %.

u21l6-7.prompt: Can you see a pause after a strong move? Up or down over the next 10 sessions?
u21l6-7.explanation: Even if it were a textbook pattern, a flag fails almost half the time according to Bulkowski. The pause doesn’t tell you how it ends.

u21l6-10.prompt: A flag normally lasts less than ____ weeks.
u21l6-10.explanation: If it lasts longer, it’s called a rectangle or a channel.

u21l7-4.prompt: You’ve bought after a breakout. Place the stop where the breakout would stop making sense: below the last relevant low.
u21l7-4.explanation: If the price drops back below the recent low, the breakout has failed and the idea is no longer valid.

u21l7-5.prompt: Another case: place the stop below the recent low.
u21l7-5.explanation: Just below the recent low, with a bit of margin: that’s where you admit the mistake.

u21l7-6.prompt: You have €10,000 and, if the breakout turns out to be false, you want to lose 1 % at most. Choose the stop and the amount.
u21l7-6.explanation: First the stop (where the breakout fails), then the amount: with a maximum risk of €100, the further away the stop, the fewer shares you can buy.

u21l7-7.prompt: Another real chart, no name, no date. Up or down over the next 10 sessions?
u21l7-7.explanation: Not even breakouts on volume guarantee anything. What you can control is where you get out if they fail and how much you lose.

u21l7-11.prompt: During the session, a stock moves above its high for the year. There are two hours to the close and volume is below average. You want to buy. What do you do?
options: I buy now, before it gets away
I buy double to make the most of the rise
I wait for the close and check whether it clears the level with volume
u21l7-11.explanation: Breakouts are confirmed by the close and the volume. Waiting a few hours costs little; falling into the trap, much more.
feedback: That's exactly how people fall for a false breakout: without a close or volume, there's no breakout yet.
More size on an unconfirmed signal multiplies the cost if it turns out to be false.
That's it: a close on the other side with above-average volume filters out many false breakouts.

u21l7-12.prompt: What do you reply to Lumi?
options: Yes: I should have removed the stop to hold on
Yes: if the stop is hit, the trade was badly set up
No: I followed the filters and the stop limited the loss; sometimes it goes wrong anyway
u21l7-12.explanation: No filter eliminates every false breakout: according to Bulkowski, the H&S fails 19 % of the time and flags around 44 %. What you control is how much the mistake costs.
feedback: Removing the stop turns a small mistake into one that can be huge.
Not necessarily: no filter eliminates every false breakout.
That's it: a good decision can turn out badly. The stop has done its job.
lines: You bought a breakout with a close and volume.
Even so, three days later it goes back inside and hits your stop.
